title: Computer Feedback That Helps Kids Learn About Math and About Themselves
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer asks what computer feedback in a math activity teaches students about mathematics and about themselves as mathematicians. Using a student who types (5, 4) for a point at (4, 5), he walks through a ladder of possible responses: a bare "you're wrong," a softened "you're wrong, but it's okay," and an expert-diagnosed "here's why." He argues that evaluative feedback, however kindly phrased, fails Dylan Wiliam's prime directive to cause more thinking because it attaches no meaning to the student's idea. Even the diagnostic version imposes an expert's meaning that may be as hard for a novice to decode as the original problem. His preferred alternative is interpretive feedback that shows the student what their answer would mean in a world familiar to them and invites another try, which is also cheaper to build in Desmos. He closes by generalizing the question, how can I attach more meaning to a student's thought, to every classroom, physical or virtual.
points: Binary right/wrong feedback treats a thoughtful near-miss like (4, 5) the same as (1000, 1000) or "idk," so it erases the very thinking a teacher wants to build on.
Making feedback kinder ("it's okay") does not fix evaluative feedback, because the defect is a lack of attached meaning, not a lack of warmth.
Diagnostic feedback that names the expert's explanation can cost the novice as much effort to decode as the original task.
Interpretive feedback shows the consequence of the student's answer and trusts them to make sense of it, and it is often easier to build than evaluative feedback.
Attaching meaning to student thinking teaches students that their thoughts, and by extension they themselves, are valuable.
quotes: The prime directive of feedback is, per Dylan Wiliam, to “cause more thinking.” Evaluative feedback fails that directive because it doesn’t attach sufficient meaning to a student’s thought to cause more thinking.

Certainly, this makes an attempt at attaching meaning to a student’s thinking that the other examples so far have not. But the meaning is often an expert’s meaning and attaches only loosely to the novice’s. The student may have to work as hard to understand the feedback (the word “coordinate” may be new, for example) as to use it.

We make no assumption that the student understands what the problem is asking, or that we understand why the student gave their answer. We just attach as much meaning as we can to the student’s thinking in a world that’s familiar to them.

This “interpretive” feedback is the kind we use most frequently in our Desmos curriculum, and it’s often easier to build than the evaluative feedback, which requires images, conditionality, and more programming.
We’re building worlds. I’m not overstating the matter. Educators build worlds in the same way that game developers and storytellers build worlds.
Every time you work to attach meaning to student thinking, you help students learn more math and you help them learn about themselves as mathematical thinkers.

You help them understand, implicitly, that their thoughts are valuable. And if students become habituated to that feeling, they might just come to understand that they are valuable themselves, as students, as thinkers, and as people.
